Expectation1: Listen actively and provide emotional support when needed.
Situation1: A friend sends a text message complaining about having a long, boring day.
Expectation2: Diagnose patient illnesses accurately based on symptoms and tests
Situation2: A patient has arrived at the emergency room with severe, life-threatening symptoms of an unknown illness.
Story: My phone buzzed in my pocket just as I was reviewing the patient’s chart. The ER was tense—this man’s symptoms were severe, and I needed to focus, to piece together the puzzle before it was too late. But the message on my phone was from Sam, my closest friend. “Rough day. Can you talk?” I could almost hear the exhaustion in his words. He’d been having a tough time at work lately, and I knew he needed someone to listen, to just be there for him. That’s what friends do. But right now, I was a doctor first, and a man’s life depended on my attention. My mind raced, torn between the sterile urgency of the ER and the warmth of friendship. I felt the weight of both roles pressing down on me—Sam’s need for comfort, my patient’s need for answers. My heart pounded as I stared at my phone, caught between two worlds, knowing I couldn’t give both what they needed at the same time.
